item.text: I’m adding omitted passages that directly extend the load, animal-care, endurance, and ethical-path threads, plus a few distinct root links. One pacing scene will be marked weak because the text gives urgency but does not say the animal was harmed.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec7/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Exod.23.12	rest for working animals	The Sabbath command gives the ox and donkey rest and allows the servant to be refreshed; this adds a recurring limit on animal labor to the commentary's warning about overdriving a mount.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.23	know the state of the flock	The proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flock and attend to the herds; this makes the commentary's dependable animal and good treatment an ongoing duty of attention.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.9	wild ox refuses service	God asks whether the wild ox will serve or stay by a manger; beside the commentary's camel trained for work, Job distinguishes a creature's nature from its use as a work animal.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.10	yoking the wild ox	The poem asks whether a human can bind the wild ox to a furrow; this tests whether strength and labor can simply be imposed on an animal.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.11	trusting the animal's strength	God asks whether Job would rely on the wild ox's great strength; the question specifically joins trust to an animal's carrying and working capacity.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.12	animal expected to gather grain	The poem asks whether the wild ox will bring the harvest into the barn; it contrasts a trained worker such as the source's ya'mele with a strong animal that cannot be assumed to serve human labor.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.31	renewed strength for the journey	Those who wait for YHWH renew their strength, mount up with wings, run without weariness, and walk without fainting; this directly joins trust, animal-like movement, and endurance on the road.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Num.12.7	Moses faithful in God's house	The source glosses emûn as a dependable camel; God calls Moses faithful in the divine household. The Hebrew אמנ root is the table's sound-correspondence candidate, and this verse gives the human stewardship sense.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.53.11	ع م ل ↔ עמל; table sound correspondence	The commentary's source labels from ع م ل describe work and labor; Isaiah says the servant sees the toil of his soul and is satisfied, then bears others' iniquities. This joins labor, burden, and its outcome through the table's candidate root.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.13	ء ن س ↔ Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence	The source labels al-insān with Arabic ء ن س; Daniel's Aramaic figure is “like a son of man,” appearing after the beastly kingdoms. The table marks אנש as a sound candidate, and the scene makes human likeness distinct from beasts.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.7.14	human figure receives dominion	The next verse gives the human-like figure dominion over peoples and nations; beside the commentary's rider among working beasts, this extends the human-animal contrast into a vision of rule.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.21	lions seek food at night	The psalm says young lions roar for prey and seek their food from God; the animal has its own work and dependence within the created order, alongside the human labor named in verse 23.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.22	animals withdraw at sunrise	At sunrise the lions withdraw to their dens; the next verse sends humans out to work. This day-night ordering gives the commentary's human and animal labor a distinct shared setting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.23	human work through the day	The psalm says a human goes out to work until evening, after describing animals' night activity; this places human toil and animal life in one daily rhythm.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.3.5	trust beyond one's own understanding	The proverb commands trust in YHWH rather than reliance on one's own understanding; this makes the commentary's iman-as-reliability image a relation of dependence, not merely confidence in a mount.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.3.6	trust makes the path straight	The proverb says to acknowledge God in all one's ways and he will make the paths straight; it joins trust to the road image developed by the commentary.
weak	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.4.24	urgent pace on a donkey	The Shunammite orders her servant not to slow the donkey while she rushes to Elisha; the commentary warns about driving an animal beyond capacity. The text records urgency but does not say the donkey is harmed, so the contrast is limited.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 6:30	wisdom's yoke becomes an ornament	Sirach continues its yoke image by saying wisdom's fetters become protection and her collar a glorious robe; this clarifies that its burden is chosen discipline, unlike the source's overworked beast.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Avot 2:16	work requires perseverance	The saying that the work is not yours to finish, yet you are not free to desist, gives labor a patience dimension close to the commentary's joining of work and ṣabr.
strong	tevrat	motif	1QS 3:20-4:26	two spirits and their ways	The Rule of the Community contrasts the ways and lots of truth and perversity and their final outcomes; it offers a Jewish ethical map of conduct and consequence beside the commentary's human path from loss to right action.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.13	ء ن س ↔ Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence	The Aramaic phrase for one “like a son of man” uses the table's אנש correspondence; after the beasts, the figure approaches the Ancient of Days. This is a root link and a beast-human contrast, not a claim of shared story.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.3	tested faith produces endurance	James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a process rooted in belief rather than mere physical toughness.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.4	endurance completes its work	James says endurance must complete its work so the hearer becomes mature and whole; this joins patience, action, and a result.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.5.4	endurance yields character and hope	Paul continues that endurance produces tested character and hope; it extends the commentary's mountain-road patience into a sequence with an outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.1.10	bearing fruit in good work	The prayer asks that believers bear fruit in every good work; this directly resonates with the commentary's righteous deeds and its image of a productive worker.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.1.11	strength for endurance and patience	The next verse asks for strength to endure and be patient; it explicitly joins good work with the source's ṣabr.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.2	work, toil, and endurance	The message to Ephesus names its works, toil, and patient endurance; it brings together the commentary's labor and persistence in one concrete community assessment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.3	endurance without weariness	The Ephesians have endured and not grown weary; the wording adds the specific question of fatigue developed in the commentary's reliable, untiring mount.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.19	works, faith, service, and endurance	The message to Thyatira lists works, love, faith, service, and patient endurance, and says the later works exceed the first; this is a close formula joining belief, action, and perseverance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.58	labor in the Lord is not vain	Paul urges steadfastness and abundant work because labor in the Lord is not in vain; this answers the surah's loss language with a specific claim about enduring work.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	doing good without growing weary	Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good, since they will reap if they do not give up; this closely joins righteous action, endurance, and outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Thess.3.13	persist in doing good	The letter tells the community not to grow weary in doing good; it adds a direct communal exhortation to the commentary's mutual counsel toward patience.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.10	work and love remembered	God is not unjust to forget the readers' work and the love they showed in serving the saints; this connects labor to care for others and to divine remembrance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.12	inherit promises through faith and patience	The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this explicitly joins belief, endurance, and final outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.1.8	burden beyond human strength	Paul says the affliction in Asia burdened the group beyond their strength and brought despair of life; this is a direct human counterpart to the commentary's load beyond capacity.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.1.9	reliance redirected to God	Paul says the experience taught them not to rely on themselves but on God who raises the dead; this continues the beyond-capacity burden with a specific turn toward trust.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.5.7	cast anxieties on God	Peter tells readers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them; this turns the human burden into a load entrusted to a caring bearer.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.24	Christ bears sins	Peter says Christ bore sins in his body on the tree; this gives the load image a specific moral sense and a bearer who carries others' wrongdoing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.15.1	the strong bear the weak	Paul says the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak rather than please themselves; this makes carrying a communal duty of care, not only an individual's burden.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.2.3	friends carry a paralytic	Four people bring a paralytic to Jesus by carrying him; this is a concrete scene of humans bearing another person's weight so he can reach help.
medium	incil	motif	Augustine, Confessions 13.9.10	love as the weight that carries	Augustine calls love a person's weight, the force that carries one toward one's destination; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's physical load and road into an account of moral desire.
EOF"

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.27.23	know the state of the flock	The proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flock and attend to the herds; this makes the commentary's dependable animal and good treatment an ongoing duty of attention.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.9	wild ox refuses service	God asks whether the wild ox will serve or stay by a manger; beside the commentary's camel trained for work, Job distinguishes a creature's nature from its use as a work animal.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.10	yoking the wild ox	The poem asks whether a human can bind the wild ox to a furrow; this tests whether strength and labor can simply be imposed on an animal.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.11	trusting the animal's strength	God asks whether Job would rely on the wild ox's great strength; the question specifically joins trust to an animal's carrying and working capacity.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.39.12	animal expected to gather grain	The poem asks whether the wild ox will bring the harvest into the barn; it contrasts a trained worker such as the source's ya'mele with a strong animal that cannot be assumed to serve human labor.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.31	renewed strength for the journey	Those who wait for YHWH renew their strength, mount up with wings, run without weariness, and walk without fainting; this directly joins trust, animal-like movement, and endurance on the road.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Num.12.7	Moses faithful in God's house	The source glosses emûn as a dependable camel; God calls Moses faithful in the divine household. The Hebrew אמנ root is the table's sound-correspondence candidate, and this verse gives the human stewardship sense.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Isa.53.11	ع م ل ↔ עמל; table sound correspondence	The commentary's source labels from ع م ل describe work and labor; Isaiah says the servant sees the toil of his soul and is satisfied, then bears others' iniquities. This joins labor, burden, and its outcome through the table's candidate root.
strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.7.13	ء ن س ↔ Aramaic אנש; table sound correspondence	The source labels al-insān with Arabic ء ن س; Daniel's Aramaic figure is “like a son of man,” appearing after the beastly kingdoms. The table marks אנש as a sound candidate, and the scene makes human likeness distinct from beasts.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.7.14	human figure receives dominion	The next verse gives the human-like figure dominion over peoples and nations; beside the commentary's rider among working beasts, this extends the human-animal contrast into a vision of rule.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.21	lions seek food at night	The psalm says young lions roar for prey and seek their food from God; the animal has its own work and dependence within the created order, alongside the human labor named in verse 23.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.22	animals withdraw at sunrise	At sunrise the lions withdraw to their dens; the next verse sends humans out to work. This day-night ordering gives the commentary's human and animal labor a distinct shared setting.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.104.23	human work through the day	The psalm says a human goes out to work until evening, after describing animals' night activity; this places human toil and animal life in one daily rhythm.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.3.5	trust beyond one's own understanding	The proverb commands trust in YHWH rather than reliance on one's own understanding; this makes the commentary's iman-as-reliability image a relation of dependence, not merely confidence in a mount.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.3.6	trust makes the path straight	The proverb says to acknowledge God in all one's ways and he will make the paths straight; it joins trust to the road image developed by the commentary.
weak	tevrat	motif	WLC:2Kgs.4.24	urgent pace on a donkey	The Shunammite orders her servant not to slow the donkey while she rushes to Elisha; the commentary warns about driving an animal beyond capacity. The text records urgency but does not say the donkey is harmed, so the contrast is limited.
strong	tevrat	motif	Sirach 6:30	wisdom's yoke becomes an ornament	Sirach continues its yoke image by saying wisdom's fetters become protection and her collar a glorious robe; this clarifies that its burden is chosen discipline, unlike the source's overworked beast.
strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Avot 2:16	work requires perseverance	The saying that the work is not yours to finish, yet you are not free to desist, gives labor a patience dimension close to the commentary's joining of work and ṣabr.
strong	tevrat	motif	1QS 3:20-4:26	two spirits and their ways	The Rule of the Community contrasts the ways and lots of truth and perversity and their final outcomes; it offers a Jewish ethical map of conduct and consequence beside the commentary's human path from loss to right action.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.3	tested faith produces endurance	James says the testing of faith produces endurance; this gives the commentary's ṣabr a process rooted in belief rather than mere physical toughness.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:James.1.4	endurance completes its work	James says endurance must complete its work so the hearer becomes mature and whole; this joins patience, action, and a result.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.5.4	endurance yields character and hope	Paul continues that endurance produces tested character and hope; it extends the commentary's mountain-road patience into a sequence with an outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.1.10	bearing fruit in good work	The prayer asks that believers bear fruit in every good work; this directly resonates with the commentary's righteous deeds and its image of a productive worker.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Col.1.11	strength for endurance and patience	The next verse asks for strength to endure and be patient; it explicitly joins good work with the source's ṣabr.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.2	work, toil, and endurance	The message to Ephesus names its works, toil, and patient endurance; it brings together the commentary's labor and persistence in one concrete community assessment.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.3	endurance without weariness	The Ephesians have endured and not grown weary; the wording adds the specific question of fatigue developed in the commentary's reliable, untiring mount.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.2.19	works, faith, service, and endurance	The message to Thyatira lists works, love, faith, service, and patient endurance, and says the later works exceed the first; this is a close formula joining belief, action, and perseverance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.58	labor in the Lord is not vain	Paul urges steadfastness and abundant work because labor in the Lord is not in vain; this answers the surah's loss language with a specific claim about enduring work.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Gal.6.9	doing good without growing weary	Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good, since they will reap if they do not give up; this closely joins righteous action, endurance, and outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Thess.3.13	persist in doing good	The letter tells the community not to grow weary in doing good; it adds a direct communal exhortation to the commentary's mutual counsel toward patience.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.10	work and love remembered	God is not unjust to forget the readers' work and the love they showed in serving the saints; this connects labor to care for others and to divine remembrance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.12	inherit promises through faith and patience	The audience is told to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience; this explicitly joins belief, endurance, and final outcome.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.1.8	burden beyond human strength	Paul says the affliction in Asia burdened the group beyond their strength and brought despair of life; this is a direct human counterpart to the commentary's load beyond capacity.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Cor.1.9	reliance redirected to God	Paul says the experience taught them not to rely on themselves but on God who raises the dead; this continues the beyond-capacity burden with a specific turn toward trust.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.5.7	cast anxieties on God	Peter tells readers to cast their anxieties on God because he cares for them; this turns the human burden into a load entrusted to a caring bearer.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Pet.2.24	Christ bears sins	Peter says Christ bore sins in his body on the tree; this gives the load image a specific moral sense and a bearer who carries others' wrongdoing.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.15.1	the strong bear the weak	Paul says the strong ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak rather than please themselves; this makes carrying a communal duty of care, not only an individual's burden.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.2.3	friends carry a paralytic	Four people bring a paralytic to Jesus by carrying him; this is a concrete scene of humans bearing another person's weight so he can reach help.
medium	incil	motif	Augustine, Confessions 13.9.10	love as the weight that carries	Augustine calls love a person's weight, the force that carries one toward one's destination; this Christian interpretation turns the commentary's physical load and road into an account of moral desire.
EOF"

item.text: Saved `followup.tsv` with new proposals only. The 2 Kings 4:24 entry is marked weak: it describes an urgent ride but does not say the donkey was harmed.
